name: Château La Tour du Pin Figeac
text:
## Château La Tour du Pin Figeac

**Where to find it:** I don't know of a current listing at BC Liquor, Alberta retailers or the LCBO, and I couldn't confirm one. Your list gives no vintage or price, so I've covered the vintages that critics have reviewed.

### The region

This wine comes from the far western edge of [Saint-Émilion](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Saint-Emilion,+Gironde,+France&t=k), on the right bank of Bordeaux, where the vineyards run up against [Pomerol](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Pomerol,+Gironde,+France&t=k). It is one of many estates in this corner of the appellation that were carved out of the original Figeac estate, in a zone where limestone and sand give way to gravel and clay.

The neighbours are famous. The estate sits on the Pomerol border, between Cheval Blanc and La Tour Figeac. You can look down on [Château Cheval Blanc](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+Cheval+Blanc,+Saint-Emilion,+France&t=k) and [Château Figeac](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+Figeac,+Saint-Emilion,+France&t=k) from above, and the estate itself is [here](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+La+Tour+du+Pin+Figeac,+Saint-Emilion,+France&t=k).

### The producer

The estate belongs to the Giraud family, who trade as Giraud-Bélivier. You can read about it on [Wikipedia's article on the estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_La_Tour_du_Pin_Figeac_(Giraud-B%C3%A9livier)), which I opened. That article says M. G. Bélivier bought it in 1923 and the Giraud family acquired it in 1972. The [Guide Hachette](https://www.hachette-vins.com/guide-vins/les-vins/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-1998-2002/20023884/) instead says the family has owned it since 1923, so the sources disagree slightly on dates.

The family runs it from their Pomerol property. The contact address is Château Le Caillou, 41 rue de Catusseau, Pomerol ([satellite view of Catusseau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+Le+Caillou,+Catusseau,+Pomerol,+France&t=k)).

The estate's standing has slipped. It was a Grand Cru Classé in the original Saint-Émilion classification, lost that status in 2006, had the decision reversed in 2008, then was left out of the 2012 classification, and its appeal failed. Today it is sold as plain Saint-Émilion Grand Cru, which is a different and lower rank than Grand Cru Classé. ([Saint-Émilion classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Classification+of+Saint-%C3%89milion+wine&go=Go))

### The grapes

The vineyard covers 11 hectares, and the wine is usually about 75% [Merlot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Merlot&go=Go) and 25% [Cabernet Franc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Cabernet+Franc&go=Go). Wine Collector's profile lists soils of clay, sand and gravel, vines averaging 40 years old, and about 64,000 bottles a year.

Merlot gives the soft, plummy body. Cabernet Franc adds fragrance, a herbal edge and freshness, which is the classic right-bank formula.

### What the critics say

Reviews are thin. This is a modest, traditional estate, and the big critics rarely publish full notes on it. Here is everything I could verify.

**2018 — Andreas Larsson, 92 points.** [Andreas Larsson](https://www.andreas-larsson.com/tasting/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-2018/) (a former Best Sommelier of the World) tasted it in 2021. He found blackcurrant, dark berries, sage and tobacco with polished oak, a medium-weight but dense palate, fine tannins, freshness and good length. [Vertdevin](https://vertdevin.com/en/vins/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-2018-saint-emilion-grand-cru-2/) scored the 2018 at 90–91 (15.5/20) from barrel.

**2020 — Vertdevin, 91 points (15.5+/20).** Vertdevin's taster rated the 2020 from barrel in May 2021, describing fresh dark berries and plum with pepper and violet. [See the page](https://vertdevin.com/en/vins/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-2020-saint-emilion-grand-cru-2/). [James Suckling](https://www.jamessuckling.com/tasting-notes/152355/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-st-emilion-2020) also reviewed the 2020, calling it spicy and salty with blueberry and chocolate and a medium body. His score is behind a paywall, so I can't give it.

**2016 — Vertdevin, 89 points.** The 2016 received 14.75+/20, or 89/100, in a December 2025 tasting. [See the page](https://vertdevin.com/en/vins/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-2016-saint-emilion-grand-cru-2).

**2010 — Robert Parker / Wine Advocate, 92 points.** Wine Collector shows a Wine Advocate score of 92 for the 2010, tasted in 2013, with a drinking window of 2013–2028. [See the page](https://www.winecollector.com/wine.aspx?wvi=194980). I could not see the note itself.

**2009 and 2012 — Andreas Larsson, 89 and 88.** He found the 2009 traditional and fairly elegant, with fresh red fruit, firm tannin and long persistence, and advised several more years in bottle when he tasted it in 2012. [2009 page](https://www.andreas-larsson.com/tasting/chateau-la-tour-du-pin-figeac-2009/). His site lists the 2012 at 88.

**CellarTracker community, 2008: 86–89 points.** On [CellarTracker](https://www.cellartracker.com/m/wines/1070476), five tasters scored the 2008 between 86 and 89 from 2016 to 2022. They liked the cedar, cassis and leather nose, but several found the palate short on fruit, with drying tannins, and advised drinking it up. One taster put the 2010 at 92 alongside it, calling the 2010 the clear winner.

**The overall picture:** good vintages (2010, 2018, 2020) land around 90–92, and weaker ones (2008, 2012) around 86–89. Critics describe it as a classic, medium-bodied, somewhat old-school Saint-Émilion rather than a plush modern one.

### Practical note

**Drink or cellar:** 2008 to 2012 should be drunk now. The 2016 and 2018 are in a good window now and should hold until about 2030. The 2020 can wait two or three more years.

**Decant:** Give younger bottles (2016 onward) about an hour in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Decanter&go=Go). Older bottles (2012 and earlier) will have sediment, so stand them upright for a day and decant gently just before serving.

**Temperature:** iDealwine recommends serving at 16 °C, which is cool room temperature. Twenty minutes in the fridge does it.

**Dishes:**
- [Tournedos Rossini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Tournedos+Rossini&go=Go), which iDealwine lists among its suggested pairings.
- Roast [duck breast (magret)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Magret&go=Go) with cherries or a red-wine reduction, which suits the Merlot fruit.
- A Pyrenean sheep's cheese such as [Ossau-Iraty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Ossau-Iraty&go=Go). The Guide Hachette suggested a Pyrenees cheese for the 2000 vintage.

### From the history books

- **1879 — The split from Figeac.** Until 1879 this land was part of the Figeac estate. It became Château La Tour Figeac, which was later divided into this estate and a second one of the same name owned by the Moueix family. ([Château Figeac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Ch%C3%A2teau+Figeac&go=Go))
- **1923 — The Bélivier purchase.** M. G. Bélivier bought the estate in 1923, and the Giraud family acquired it in 1972.
- **2006 — Cheval Blanc buys the twin.** LVMH, owner of Cheval Blanc, bought the Moueix estate in 2006 and dropped both "Moueix" and "Figeac" from its name. ([LVMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=LVMH&go=Go), [Moueix family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Moueix&go=Go))
- **2006 to 2012 — The classification battles.** The estate was demoted in 2006, reinstated in 2008, and excluded in 2012 with no successful appeal. The Wine Doctor notes that the 2006 classification was itself later annulled.
- **After 2011 — The twin vanishes.** The former Moueix estate disappeared after the 2011 vintage. About 1.4 hectares of gravelly Merlot went into Cheval Blanc, the first addition to that vineyard in more than 140 years, and the rest was replanted to white grapes.

### Curious details

**Two châteaux, one name.** For decades two neighbouring estates carried exactly the same name, and buyers told them apart only by the owner's name in brackets. Because the Moueix estate was absorbed, the Giraud property is now the only Château La Tour du Pin Figeac.

**Its twin's vines now make white wine.** The sandy, fine-gravel part of the old Moueix vineyard was converted to Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, and it now supplies Le Petit Cheval Blanc, Cheval Blanc's white wine. So your bottle's next-door "twin" now grows white grapes for one of Bordeaux's most famous names. ([Sauvignon Blanc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Sauvignon+blanc&go=Go), [Sémillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=S%C3%A9millon&go=Go))

**The soils change here.** This western strip is where Saint-Émilion's limestone and sand give way to gravel and clay, the same type of ground that makes neighbouring Pomerol famous. Gravel drains well and holds warmth, which helps Cabernet Franc ripen. ([Gravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Gravel&go=Go), [Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Clay&go=Go))

**Iron-rich soils at the family's Pomerol estate.** The Guide Hachette notes that Le Caillou, the family's Pomerol property, takes its name from the land register and sits on sandy gravels with "crasse de fer", the iron-rich hardpan typical of Pomerol.

**Don't confuse it with La Tour Figeac.** Château La Tour Figeac, without "du Pin", is a different estate. It still holds Grand Cru Classé status and earns higher scores. When you shop, make sure the label says "du Pin".

## Ranking by what reviewers say
1. **Château La Tour du Pin Figeac**: added by name, not on your store lists. Its best-supported score is 92 from Andreas Larsson for the 2018 (also Wine Advocate 92 for the 2010). My own rating is 89 for the 2018: a solid, traditional Saint-Émilion, but a notch below its classified neighbours.
